original_japanese:
秋の田の
かりほの庵の
苫をあらみ
わが衣手は
露にぬれつつ
original_romaji:
Aki no ta no
Kario no io no
Toma no arami
Waga koromo de wa
Tsuyu ni furitsutsu
dickens_text_1866:
My lowly hut is thatched with straw
From fields where rice-sheaves frequent stand,
Now autumn's harvest well-nigh o'er,
Collected by my toiling hand:
Through tatter'd roof the sky I view,
My clothes are wet with falling dew
noguchi_text_1907:
My clothes wet with the midnight dews—
Through the roof mat,
In this temporal hut,
For our harvest.
porter_text_1909:
Out in the fields this autumn day
They're busy reaping grain ;
I sought for shelter ’neath this roof,
But fear I sought in vain,—
My sleeve is wet with rain.
maccauley_text_1917:
Coarse the rush-mat roof
Sheltering the harvest-hut
Of the autumn rice-field;--
And my sleeves are growing wet
With the moisture dripping through.

original_japanese:
春過ぎて
夏来にけらし
白妙の
衣ほすてふ
天の香具山
original_romaji:
Haru sugite
Natsu ki ni kerashi
Shirotae no
Koromo hosu cho
Ama no Kaguyama
dickens_text_1866:
The pleasant spring hath passed away,
Now summer follows close, I ween,
And Ama's secret summit may
In all its grandeur now be seen;
Of yore the drying ground,
Whitened with angels' robes, spread far around.
noguchi_text_1907:
Has Spring passed away?
Did Summer already come?
Lo, Kagu Yama!  There
The white gowns are seen being dried.
porter_text_1909:
The spring has gone, the summer's come,
And I can just descry
The peak of Ama-no-kagu,
Where angels of the sky
Spread their white robes to dry.
maccauley_text_1917:
Spring, it seems, has passed,
And the summer come again;
For the silk-white robes,
So 'tis said, are spread to dry
On the "Mount of Heaven's Perfume."

original_japanese:
あしびきの
山鳥の尾の
しだり尾の
ながながし夜を
ひとりかもねむ
original_romaji:
Ashibiki no
Yamadori no o no
Shidari o no
Naganagashi yo o
Hitori ka mo nen
dickens_text_1866:
The hill-side fowl his long-drooped tail
Sweeps o'er the ground--so drags the night.
My lonely plight
I mourn--my sleepless wretchedness bewail.
noguchi_text_1907:
What a long night!
How could I sleep alone!
How the night drags!—(Dragging
As a mountain fowl's long-dropped tail!)
porter_text_1909:
Long is the mountain pheasant's tail
That curves down in its flight;
But longer still, it seems to me,
Left in my lonely plight,
Is this unending night.
maccauley_text_1917:
Ah! the foot-drawn trail
Of the mountain-pheasant's tail
Drooped like down-curved branch!--
Through this long, long-dragging night
Must I keep my couch alone?

original_japanese:
田子の浦に
打ち出でてみれば
白妙の
富士の高嶺に
雪はふりつつ
original_romaji:
Tago no Ura ni
Uchi idete mireba
Shirotae no
Fuji no takane ni
Yuki wa furi tsutsu
dickens_text_1866:
From where my home,--
My lonely home, --onTago's shore
Doth stand, the wandering eye may roam
O'er Fusiyama's summit hoar,
Whose lofty brow
Is whitened by th' new-fallen snow.
noguchi_text_1907:
From Tago Ura,
I behold Fuji's white summit,—
Over the high summit,
The snow falling and falling on.
porter_text_1909:
I started off along the shore,
The sea shore at Tago,
And saw the white and glist’ning peak
Of Fuji all aglow
Through falling flakes of snow.
maccauley_text_1917:
When to Tago's coast
I the way have gone, and see
Perfect whiteness laid
On Mount Fuji's lofty peak
By the drift of falling snow.

original_japanese:
奥山に
紅葉ふみわけ
鳴く鹿の
声きく時ぞ
秋は悲しき
original_romaji:
Okuyama ni
Momiji fumiwake
Naku shika no
Koe kiku toki zo
Aki wa kanashiki
dickens_text_1866:
Now 'mid the hills the Momiji
Is trampled down 'neath hoof of deer,
Whose plaintive cries continually
Are heard both far and near;
My shivering frame
Now autumn's piercing chills doth blame.
noguchi_text_1907:
How sad is Autumn,
When you hear the deer's cry.
With his hoofs upon the maple leaves,
Amid the deeper hill!
porter_text_1909:
Hear the stag's pathetic call
Far up the mountain side,
While tramping o'er the maple leaves
Wind-scattered far and wide
This sad, sad autumn tide.
maccauley_text_1917:
In the mountain depths,
Treading through the crimson leaves,
Cries the wandering stag.
When I hear the lonely cry,
Sad,--how sad--the autumn is!

original_japanese:
かささぎの
渡せる橋に
置く霜の
白きを見れば
夜ぞふけにける
original_romaji:
Kasasagi no
Wataseru hashi ni
Oku shimo no
Shiroki o mireba
Yo zo fuke ni keru
dickens_text_1866:
Upon the bridge where ravens, aye,
Do love to pass where hoar-frost's sheen,
When hoar-frost's glittering film is seen;
I trow the break of day is nigh.
noguchi_text_1907:
Must be done the night:
Over the Kasasagi bridge in the sky,
The frost white, I see,
Is set already.
porter_text_1909:
When on the Magpies' Bridge I see
The Hoar-frost King has cast
His sparkling mantle, well I know
The night is nearly past,
Daylight approaches fast.
maccauley_text_1917:
If the "Magpie Bridge"--
Bridge by flight of magpies spanned,--
White with frost I see:--
With a deep-laid frost made white:--
Late, I know, has grown the night.

original_japanese:
天の原
ふりさけ見れば
春日なる
三笠の山に
出でし月かも
original_romaji:
Ama no hara
Furisake mireba
Kasuga naru
Mikasa no yama ni
Ideshi tsuki kamo
dickens_text_1866:
On every side the vaulted sky
I view: now will the moon have peered
I trow, above Mikasa high
In Kasuga's far-off land upreared.
noguchi_text_1907:
Behold the heavenly vastness,
The sky of the moon!
Is it not the same moon I once saw,
Out of Kasuga's Mikasa hill?
porter_text_1909:
While gazing up into the sky,
My thoughts have wandered far;
Methinks I see the rising moon
Above Mount Mikasa
At far-off Kasuga.
maccauley_text_1917:
When I look abroad
O'er the wide-stretched "Plain of Heaven,"
Is the moon the same
That on Mount Mikasa rose,
In the land of Kasuga?

original_japanese:
わが庵は
都のたつみ
しかぞすむ
世をうぢ山と
人はいふなり
original_romaji:
Waga io wa
Miyako no tatsumi
Shika zo sumu
Yo o Ujiyama to
Hito wa iu nari
dickens_text_1866:
My cabin doth in Tats'mi lie
Miako's city near
Yo-uji men my mountain call,
Yet still do I dwell here.
noguchi_text_1907:
My hut is southward of the city,
here like this I live alone:
Why, people call here Ujiyama.
(The "World-sad Hill")!
porter_text_1909:
My home is near the Capital,
My humble cottage bare
Lies south-east on
Mount Uji; so
The people all declare
My life's a 'Hill of Care'.
maccauley_text_1917:
Lowly hut is mine
South-east from the capital:--
Thus I choose to dwell;--
And the world in which I live
Men have named a "Mount of Gloom."

original_japanese:
花の色は
うつりにけりな
いたづらに
わが身世にふる
ながめせしまに
original_romaji:
Hana no iro wa
Utsuri ni keri na
Itazura ni
Waga mi yo ni furu
Nagame seshi ma ni
dickens_text_1866:
Thy love hath passed away from me
Left, desolate, forlorn--
In winter-rains how wearily
The summer past I mourn!
noguchi_text_1907:
The flowers and my love,
Passed away under the rain,
While I idly looked upon them:
Where is my yester-love?
porter_text_1909:
The blossom's tint is washed away
By heavy showers of rain;
My charms, which once I prized so much,
Are also on the wane,
Both bloomed, alas! in vain.
maccauley_text_1917:
Color of the flower
Has already passed away
While on trivial things
Vainly I have set my gaze,
In my journey through the world.

original_japanese:
これやこの
行くも帰るも
別れては
知るも知らぬも
逢坂の関
original_romaji:
Kore ya kono
Yuku mo kaeru mo
Wakarete wa
Shiru mo shiranu mo
Osaka no seki
dickens_text_1866:
Some hence towards the city haste,
Some from the city here speed by,
Here friends and strangers meet and part,
With kindly glance and careless eye;
Apt is the name it seems to me,
Ausaka gate, men give to thee.
noguchi_text_1907:
here some depart, here some return,
Once they part, and they meet here again,—
The people who know and who know not:
'Tis Ausaka Gate (the "Meeting Height Gate").
porter_text_1909:
The stranger who has travelled far,
The friend with welcome smile,
All sorts of men who come and go
Meet at this mountain stile,—
They meet and rest awhile.
maccauley_text_1917:
Truly, this is where
Travelers who go or come
Over parting ways,--
Friends or strangers,--all must meet;
'Tis the gate of "Meeting Hill."

original_japanese:
わたの原
八十島かけて
こぎ出ぬと
人には告げよ
あまのつり舟
original_romaji:
Wata no hara
Yasoshima kakete
Kogi idenu to
Hito ni wa tsugeyo
Ama no tsuri bune
dickens_text_1866:
Ye fishermen, who range the sea
In many a barque, I pray ye tell
My fellow-villagers of me--
How that far o'er vast ocean's swell
In vessel frail
Towards Yasoshima I sail.
noguchi_text_1907:
O thou, fisher's boat,
Tell men that I sailed.
Away into the eighty isles,
Into the bluest field,—the sea!
porter_text_1909:
Oh! Fishers in your little boats,
Quick! tell my men, I pray,
They'll find me at Yasoshima,
I'm being rowed away
Far off across the bay.
maccauley_text_1917:
O'er the wide, wide sea,
Towards its many distant isles,
Rowing I set forth.
This, to all the world proclaim,
O ye boats of fisher-folk!

original_japanese:
天つ風
雲のかよひ路
吹きとぢよ
乙女のすがた
しばしとどめむ
original_romaji:
Ama tsu kaze
Kumo no kayoiji
Fuki toji yo
Otome no sugata
Shibashi todomen
dickens_text_1866:
In fitful path across the sky,
By various winds of heaven forced,
Cloud-borne Otome glideth by--
Now hath the breeze its vigour lost
An instant, and her form so bright
For a fleeting moment greets my sight.
noguchi_text_1907:
O heavenly wind,
Blow and stop the road of clouds!
Let the beauties, nay, the angels,
For a while be with us!
porter_text_1909:
Oh stormy winds, bring up the clouds,
And paint the heavens grey;
Lest these fair maids of form divine
Should angel wings display,
And fly far far away.
maccauley_text_1917:
O ye Winds of Heaven!
In the paths among the clouds
Blow, and close the ways,
That we may these virgin forms
Yet a little while detain.

original_japanese:
筑波嶺の
峰より落つる
みなの川
恋ぞつもりて
淵となりぬる
original_romaji:
Tsukuba ne no
Mine yori otsuru
Minano-gawa
Koi zo tsumorite
Fuchi to nari nuru
dickens_text_1866:
The minagawa's waters fall
From Ts'kubaneyama's lofty peak:
In loving haste the waters all
For aye accumulate, and seek
The end of all their constant flow,
The sea that doth no limits know.
noguchi_text_1907:
From the Tsukuba summit,
Mina no Kawa drops down,
And the waters gathered make the depth!
Oh so is love.
porter_text_1909:
The Mina stream comes tumbling down
From Mount Tsukuba's height;
Strong as my love, it leaps into
A pool as black as night
With overwhelming might.
maccauley_text_1917:
From Tsukuba's peak,
Falling waters have become
Mina's still, full flow:
So my love has grown to be;
Like the river's quiet deeps.

original_japanese:
みちのくの
しのぶもぢずり
誰故に
乱れそめにし
我ならなくに
original_romaji:
Michinoku no
Shinobu moji-zuri
Tare yue ni
Midare some ni shi
Ware naranaku ni
dickens_text_1866:
Ah me! my soul with cares is vext,
Unnumbered, crowded, and perplext,
Than varied pattern more confus'd
On Mojidsuri fabric used,
The produce of Shinobu's loom,
Shinobu in Michinoku land;
For whose sake whose buth thine doth gloom
Hold o'er my failing heart command.
noguchi_text_1907:
Why does thy heart so stir,
Mojizuri of Michinoku's Shinobu loom?
Whom my heart does stir to?
Alas, nobody but my love!
porter_text_1909:
Ah! why does love distract my thoughts,
Disordering my will!
I'm like the pattern on the cloth
Of Michinoku hill,—
All in confusion still.
maccauley_text_1917:
Michinoku print
Of shinobu's tangled leaves!
For whose sake have I,
Like confused, begun to be?
Only yours! I can not change!

original_japanese:
君がため
春の野に出でて
若菜つむ
わが衣手に
雪はふりつつ
original_romaji:
Kimi ga tame
Haru no no ni idete
Wakana tsumu
Waga koromode ni
Yuki wa furi tsutsu
dickens_text_1866:
Thy wishes, love, have I obeyed,
And 'mid the meadows have I strayed
In this spring-time, and sought with care
The wakana plant that groweth there.
Lo on my sleeve
The falling snow its trace doth leave.
noguchi_text_1907:
For thy sake,
I come out in the Spring field,
And the wakana I gather,—
Lo, the snow-flakes falling on my gown.
porter_text_1909:
Mother, for thy sake I have been
Where the wakana grow,
To bring thee back some fresh green leaves
And see—my koromo
Is sprinkled with the snow!
maccauley_text_1917:
It is for thy sake
That I seek the fields in spring,
Gathering green herbs,
While my garment's hanging sleeves
Are with falling snow beflecked.

original_japanese:
立ち別れ
いなばの山の
峰に生ふる
まつとしきかば
今かへりこむ
original_romaji:
Tachi wakare
Inaba no yama no
Mine ni oru
Matsu to shi kikaba
Ima kaeri kon
dickens_text_1866:
Inaba's lofty range is crowned
By many a tall pine-tree;
Ah quickly were I homewards bound
If thou shouldst pine for me.
noguchi_text_1907:
Now we part.  The pine-tree grows.
There on the Inaba mountain top.
If thou shouldst say "pine"
I to you will soon return.
porter_text_1909:
If breezes on Inaba's peak
Sigh through the old pine tree,
To whisper in my lonely ears
That thou dost pine for me,—
Swiftly I'll fly to thee.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though we parted be;
If on Mount Inaba's peak
I should hear the sound
Of the pine trees growing there,
Back at once I'll make my way.

original_japanese:
千早ぶる
神代もきかず
龍田川
からくれないに
水くくるとは
original_romaji:
Chihayaburu
Kamiyo mo kikazu
Tatsuta-gawa
Kara kurenai ni
Mizu kukuru to wa
dickens_text_1866:
O Tatsta! when th' autumnal flow
I watch of thy deep, ruddy wave--
E'en when the stern gods long ago
Did rule, was ne'er beheld so brave,
So fair a stream as thine, I vow.
noguchi_text_1907:
I did not hear even in the gods' age,—
Behold Tatsuda Gawa!—
The waters were reddened so
By the autumn leaves.
porter_text_1909:
All red with leaves Tatsuta's stream
So softly purls along,
The everlasting Gods themselves,
Who judge 'twixt right and wrong,
Ne'er heard so sweet a song.
maccauley_text_1917:
I have never heard
That, e'en when the gods held sway
In the ancient days,
E'er was water bound with red
Such as here in Tatta's stream

original_japanese:
住の江の
岸による波
よるさへや
夢の通ひ路
人目よくらむ
original_romaji:
Sumi no e no
Kishi ni yoru nami
Yoru sae ya
Yume no kayoi ji
Hito me yoku ran
dickens_text_1866:
Tho' softly as the waves do break
On Suminoye's shore, I seek
To meet thee, love e'en in a dream,
To dread men's curious eyes I seem.
noguchi_text_1907:
I think of thee,
I go along the road of dream to meet thee,
How I fear people's curious eyes!
(Oh my love riding on the waves of dream!)
porter_text_1909:
To-night on Sumi-no-ye beach
The waves alone draw near;
And, as we wander by the cliffs,
No prying eyes shall peer,
No one shall dream we're here.
maccauley_text_1917:
Lo! the gathered waves
On the shore of Sumi's bay!
E'en in gathered night,
When in dreams I go to thee,
I must shun the eyes of men.

original_japanese:
難波潟
みじかき芦の
ふしのまも
あはでこの世を
過ぐしてよとや
original_romaji:
Naniwa gata
Mijikaki ashi no
Fushi no ma mo
Awade kono yo o
Sugushite yo to ya
dickens_text_1866:
Scant are the joints of Ashi reed
That grow Nanihagata nigh,
While time o'er e'en as brief space speed
Failst thou to greet my longing eye.
I fain would die!
noguchi_text_1907:
Must I pass the days and world,
Not seeing thee,
Even for a short time,—short
like the ashi joints of the Naniwa shore?
porter_text_1909:
Short as the joints of bamboo reeds
That grow beside the sea
On pebble beach at Naniwa,
I hope the time may be,
When thou ’rt away from me.
maccauley_text_1917:
Even for a space
Short as joint of tiny reed
From Naniwa's marsh,
We must never meet again
In this life? This, do you ask?

original_japanese:
わびぬれば
今はた同じ
難波なる
身をつくしても
逢はむとぞ思ふ
original_romaji:
Wabi nureba
Ima hata onaji
Naniwa naru
Mi o tsukushite mo
Awan to zo omou
dickens_text_1866:
Distracted by my misery,
How utterly forlorn am I;
Oh that I might thee once more see
Tho' it should cost my life to me!
noguchi_text_1907:
Now it will be same whatever it be.
Oh what a misery!
I might think to see thee once more
Even for my own life.
porter_text_1909:
We met but for a moment, and
I'm wretched as before;
The tide shall measure out my life,
Unless I see once more
The maid, whom I adore.
maccauley_text_1917:
Now, in dire distress,
It is all the same to me!
So, then, let us meet
Even though it costs my life
In the Bay of Naniwa.

original_japanese:
今来むと
いひしばかりに
長月の
有明の月を
待ち出でつるかな
original_romaji:
Ima kon to
Iishi bakari ni
Nagatsuki no
Ariake no tsuki o
Machi idetsuru kana
dickens_text_1866:
Oh, maiden! heedless of thy vow,
Why com'st thou not? 'Tis "long-moon" night,
And th' Ariake moon shines now,
Forgetfulless with welcome light.
noguchi_text_1907:
Now I have to wait
Only for the Naga Tsuki morning moon to appear,
But thy word of promise
To come and see me soon!
porter_text_1909:
The moon that shone the whole night through
This autumn morn I see,
As here I wait thy well-known step,
For thou didst promise me—
'I'll surely come to thee.'
maccauley_text_1917:
Just because she said,
"In a moment I will come,"
I've awaited her
E'en until the moon of dawn,
In the long month, hath appeared.

original_japanese:
吹くからに
秋の草木の
しをるれば
むべ山風を
あらしといふらむ
original_romaji:
Fuku kara ni
Aki no kusaki no
Shiorureba
Mube yama kaze o
Arashi to iuran
dickens_text_1866:
Now autumn's gales, in various freak,
On herb, on tree, destruction wreak,
And wildest roar
The gusts that down from Mube pour.
noguchi_text_1907:
Under the wind-blow,
The Autumn grasses and trees wither away.
Is it not right to call
A yama kaze “storm”?
porter_text_1909:
The mountain wind in autumn time
Is well called 'hurricane';
It hurries canes and twigs along,
And whirls them o'er the plain
To scatter them again.
maccauley_text_1917:
Since 'tis by its breath
Autumn's leaves of grass and trees
Riven are and waste,--
Men may to the mountain wind
Fitly given the name, "The Wild."

original_japanese:
月見れば
千々に物こそ
悲しけれ
わが身ひとつの
秋にはあらねど
original_romaji:
Tsuki mireba
Chiji ni mono koso
Kanashi kere
Waga mi hitotsu no
Aki ni wa aranedo
dickens_text_1866:
How oft' my glance upon the moon hath dwelt,
Her secret power my soul subdued--
Her sadd'ning influence I alone have felt,
Though all men autumn's moon have viewed.
noguchi_text_1907:
To gaze upon the moon
Is to be sad in a thousand ways,
Though all the Autumn
Is not meant to be my own self’s.
porter_text_1909:
This night the cheerless autumn moon
Doth all my mind enthrall;
But others also have their griefs,
For autumn on us all
Hath cast her gloomy pall
maccauley_text_1917:
Gaze I at the moon,
Myriad things arise in thought,
And my thoughts are sad;--
Yet, 'tis not for me alone,
That the autumn time has come.

original_japanese:
このたびは
幣もとりあへず
手向山
紅葉のにしき
神のまにまに
original_romaji:
Kono tabi wa
Nusa mo toriaezu
Tamukeyama
Momiji no nishiki
Kami no mani mani
dickens_text_1866:
This time, I ween, no need there be,
A nusa I should take with me:
The nishki of the maple-tree
Tamuke-yama thou dost show.
'Twill serve the gods full well, I trow.
noguchi_text_1907:
A nusa I could not bring with me this time,
Oh god, but the brocade of maple leaves
Of the Tamuke mountain
Will serve for thy will.
porter_text_1909:
I bring no prayers on coloured silk
To deck thy shrine to-day,
But take instead these maple leaves,
That grow at Tamuké;
Finer than silk are they.
maccauley_text_1917:
At the present time,
Since no offering I could bring,
See, Mount Tamuke!
Here are brocades of red leaves,
At the pleasure of the god.

original_japanese:
名にしおはば
逢坂山の
さねかづら
人にしられで
くるよしもがな
original_romaji:
Na ni shi owaba
Osakayama no
Sanekazura
Hito ni shirarede
Kuru yoshi mo gana
dickens_text_1866:
If thou'rt as fair as rumour thee
Doth paint, O deign my hut to grace
And may thy path as secret be
To human eye as is the trace
Of Sanekads'ra 'mid
Osaka-yama's forests hid!
noguchi_text_1907:
Is there no way to come as secret
As the trace of a sanekatsura vine
Of the Osaka mountain?
(Oh, reel of the vine!)
porter_text_1909:
Hear thou art as modest as
The little creeping spray
Upon Mount Ōsaka, which hides
Beneath the grass; then, pray,
Wander with me to-day.
maccauley_text_1917:
If thy name be true,
Trailing vine of "Meeting Hill,"
Is there not some way
Whereby, without ken of men,
I can draw thee to my side?

original_japanese:
小倉山
峰のもみじ葉
心あらば
今ひとたびの
みゆきまたなむ
original_romaji:
Ogurayama
Mine no momijiba
Kokoro araba
Ima hitotabi no
Miyuki matanan
dickens_text_1866:
The redd'ning leaves of th' momiji
That on Ogura's summit grow,
How pleasant 'tis their tints to see!
Ah! did they but their beauty know,
They would linger till there pass'd again
Our Emperor's miyuki train.
noguchi_text_1907:
The maple leaves on the Ogura mountain top,
If they knew, would wait
For the Emperor’s miyuki train
To pass once more.
porter_text_1909:
The maples of Mount Ogura,
If they could understand,
Would keep their brilliant leaves, until
The Ruler of this land
Pass with his royal band.
maccauley_text_1917:
If the maple leaves
On the ridge of Ogura
Have the gift of mind,
They will longingly await
One more august pilgrimage.

original_japanese:
みかの原
わきてながるる
泉川
いつ見きとてか
恋しかるらむ
original_romaji:
Mika no Hara
Wakite nagaruru
Izumi-gawa
Itsu mi kitote ka
Koishi karuran
dickens_text_1866:
Lo Idsmi's boiling waters flow
With tumult vast, through Mika's plain;
My mind doth like confusion know,
A wretched prey to lover's pain.
noguchi_text_1907:
Like the Izumi stream
Boiling down through the Mika plain,
Oh, my heart!
When did I see her to love so!
porter_text_1909:
Oh! rippling River Izumi,
That flows through Mika plain,
Why should the maid I saw but now
And soon shall see again
Torment my love-sick brain?
maccauley_text_1917:
Over Mika's plain,
Gushing forth and flowing free,
Is Izumi's stream.
I know not if we have met:
Why, then, do I long for her?

original_japanese:
山里は
冬ぞさびしさ
まさりける
人めも草も
かれぬとおもへ
original_romaji:
Yama-zato wa
Fuyu zo sabishisa
Masari keru
Hitome mo kusa mo
Karenu to omoeba
dickens_text_1866:
The hamlet bosom'd 'mid the hills
Aye lonely is; in winter-time
Its solitude with mis'ry fills
My mind, for now the rig'rous clime
Hath banished every herb and tree
And every human face from me.
noguchi_text_1907:
The mountain village in Winter
Will be lonelier. Oh, to think
That every human face and grass
Are to die away from me!
porter_text_1909:
The mountain village solitude
In winter time I dread;
It seems as if, when friends are gone,
And trees their leaves have shed,
All men and plants are dead.
maccauley_text_1917:
Winter loneliness
In a mountain hamlet grows
Only deeper, when
Guests are gone, and leaves and grass
Withered are;--so runs my thought.

original_japanese:
心あてに
折らばや折らむ
初霜の
おきまどはせる
白菊の花
original_romaji:
Kokoroate ni
Orabaya oran
Hatsushimo no
Oki madowaseru
Shiragiku no hana
dickens_text_1866:
I had to pluck thee, flower,--thought--
To pluck thee, flower, in vain I sought:
The earliest hoar-frost feigning thee,
Fair Shiragiku, cheated me.
noguchi_text_1907:
How shall I pluck
The white chrysanthemum?
’Tis hard To choose one from those
With the earliest frost thickly set.
porter_text_1909:
It was a white chrysanthemum
I came to take away;
But, which are coloured, which are white,
I'm half afraid to say,
So thick the frost to-day!
maccauley_text_1917:
If it were my wish
White chrysanthemum to cull;--
Puzzled by the frost
Of the early autumn time,
I by chance might pluck the flower.

original_japanese:
有明の
つれなくみえし
別れより
暁ばかり
うきものはなし
original_romaji:
Ariake no
Tsurenaku mieshi
Wakare yori
Akatsuki bakari
Uki mono wa nashi
dickens_text_1866:
The Ariake-moonbeams wills
In th' morning heaven linger still;
While I from thee--how hard the smart--
By Akadski compelled, must part.
noguchi_text_1907:
There’s nothing more hard
Than an early morning parting.
Oh, how heartless
The morning moon does appear!
porter_text_1909:
I hate the cold unfriendly moon,
That shines at early morn;
And nothing seems so sad and grey,
When I am left forlorn,
As day's returning dawn.
maccauley_text_1917:
Like the morning moon,
Cold, unpitying was my love.
Since that parting hour,
Nothing I dislike so much
As the breaking light of day.

original_japanese:
朝ぼらけ
有明の月と
みるまでに
吉野の里に
ふれる白雪
original_romaji:
Asaborake
Ariake no tsuki to
Miru made ni
Yoshino no sato ni
Fureru shirayuki
dickens_text_1866:
Now clearly broke the dawning day,
Ariake moon I thought to see--
The newly-fallen snow that lay
Bound Yoshino deceived me.
The whiten'd hill-side seemed
As tho thereon the moonlight streamed.
noguchi_text_1907:
I thought it might be
The shadow of the morning moon,
But the white snows fall
On the yoshino village.
porter_text_1909:
Surely the morning moon, I thought,
Has bathed the hill in light
But, no; I see it is the snow
That, falling in the night,
Has made Yoshino white.
maccauley_text_1917:
At the break of day,
Just as though the morning moon
Lightened the dim scene,
Yoshino's fair hamlet lay
In a haze of falling snow.

original_japanese:
山川に
風のかけたる
しがらみは
流れもあへぬ
紅葉なりけり
original_romaji:
Yama kawa ni
Kaze no kaketaru
Shigarami wa
Nagare mo aenu
Momiji nari keri
dickens_text_1866:
The winds of autumn have amassed
Dried withered leaves in ruddy heaps,
Have them in th' mountain-torret cast,
Whose stream in stony channel sweeps;
Amid the rocks that bar the way
The Mom-ji's reddened leaves delay.
noguchi_text_1907:
The hurdle that the wind built
Over the mountain river
Is nothing but the maple leaves
Not run down.
porter_text_1909:
The stormy winds of yesterday
The maple branches shook;
And see! a mass of crimson leaves
Has lodged within that nook,
And choked the mountain brook.
maccauley_text_1917:
In a mountain stream,
Builded by the busy wind,
Is a wattled-barrier drawn.
Yet 'tis only maple leaves
Powerless to flow away.

original_japanese:
久方の
光のどけき
春の日に
しづ心なく
花のちるらむ
original_romaji:
Hisakata no
Hikari nodokeki
Haru no hi ni
Shizu-gokoro naku
Hana no chiruran
dickens_text_1866:
'Tis a pleasant day of merry spring,
No bitter frosts are threatening
No storm-winds blow, no rain-clouds low'r,
The sun shines bright on high,
Yet thou, poor trembling little flow'r,
Dost wither away and die.
noguchi_text_1907:
’Tis the Spring day
With lovely far-away light.
Why the flowers must fall
With hearts unquiet?
porter_text_1909:
The spring has come, and once again
The sun shines in the sky;
So gently smile the heavens, that
It almost makes me cry,
When blossoms droop and die.
maccauley_text_1917:
In the cheerful light
Of the ever-shining Sun,
In the days of spring;
Why, with ceaseless, restless haste
Falls the cherry's new-blown bloom?

original_japanese:
誰をかも
知る人にせむ
高砂の
松もむかしの
友ならなくに
original_romaji:
Tare o ka mo
Shiru hito ni sen
Takasago no
Matsu mo mukashi no
Tomo nara naku ni
dickens_text_1866:
Of old companions bereft
Men's friendship more I may not seek,
Nought but the ancient pine-trees left,
That grow on Takasago's peak,
Comrades of many a year now gone,
But not the friends for whom I mourn.
noguchi_text_1907:
Who shall I make my friend?
Even the Takasago pine-tree
Could not remain
As an old friend of mine.
porter_text_1909:
Gone are my old familiar friends,
The men I used to know;
Yet still on Takasago beach
The same old pine trees-grow,
That I knew long ago.
maccauley_text_1917:
Whom then are there now,
In my age (so far advanced)
I can hold as friends?
Even Takasago's pines
Are not friends of former days.

original_japanese:
人はいさ
心も知らず
ふるさとは
花ぞむかしの
香に匂ひける
original_romaji:
Hito wa isa
Kokoro mo shirazu
Furusato wa
Hana zo mukashi no
Ka ni nioi keru
dickens_text_1866:
The comrades of my early days
Their former friend indifferent view,
Who with a wondering eye doth gaze
On th' village that olf he knw
So well. O flower! thy fragrancy
Alone familiar seems to me.
noguchi_text_1907:
I know now what one thinks
Of me. But at the home
The flowers are perfumed
In fragrance old and same.
porter_text_1909:
The village of my youth is gone,
New faces meet my gaze;
But still the blossoms at thy gate,
Whose perfume scents the ways,
Recall my childhood's days.
maccauley_text_1917:
No! no! As for man,
How his heart is none can tell,
But the plum's sweet flower
In my birthplace, as of yore,
Still emits the same perfume.

original_japanese:
夏の夜は
まだ宵ながら
明けぬるを
雲のいづくに
月やどるらむ
original_romaji:
Natsu no yo wa
Mada yoi nagara
Akenuru o
Kumo no izuko ni
Tsuki yadoruran
dickens_text_1866:
'Twas a summer's night, I scarcely thought
The evening hours had passed away
When dawn broke; long the moon I'd sought,
Now kne where 'mid the clouds she lay.
noguchi_text_1907:
The Summer night will break
When the evening scarcely passed,
What cloud will the moon
Take as her lodging place?
porter_text_1909:
Too short the lovely summer night,
Too soon ’tis passed away;
I watched to see behind which cloud
The moon would chance to stay,
And here's the dawn of day!
maccauley_text_1917:
In the summer night,
While the evening still seems here,
Lo! the dawn has come.
In what region of the clouds
Has the wandering moon found place?

original_japanese:
白露を
風のふきしく
秋の野は
つらぬきとめぬ
玉ぞちりける
original_romaji:
Shiratsuyu o
Kaze no fukishiku
Aki no no wa
Tsuranuki tomenu
Tama zo chiri keru
dickens_text_1866:
Now dew-drops sparkling o'er the moor are seen,
The autumn gust sweeps howling by,
Scarce lurks as instant 'mid the reeds I ween:
In timid show'r the dew-drops fly,
And, scatter o'er the grass, there lie.
noguchi_text_1907:
Over the Autumn field
Of white dews, in gust,
Lo, the stringless pearls
Are scattered away.
porter_text_1909:
This lovely morn the dewdrops flash
Like diamonds on the grass—
A blaze of sparkling jewels! But
The autumn wind, alas!
Scatters them as I pass.
maccauley_text_1917:
In the autumn fields,
When the heedless wind blows by
O'er the pure-white dew,
How the myriad unstrung gems
Everywhere are scattered round!

original_japanese:
忘らるる
身をば思はず
誓ひてし
人の命の
惜しくもあるかな
original_romaji:
Wasuraruru
Mi o ba omowazu
Chikaite shi
Hito no inochi no
Oshiku mo aru kana
dickens_text_1866:
A solemn oath tou swor'st with me,
I dreamt thou wouldest constant be--
Forgotten, scorned the penalty
Of death I almost cry on thee.
noguchi_text_1907:
I do not mind of myself
To be forgotten by him,
But for his own life’s sake
I have to grieve.
porter_text_1909:
My broken heart I don't lament,
To destiny I bow;
But thou hast broken solemn oaths,—
I pray the Gods may now
Absolve thee from thy vow.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though forgotten now,
For myself I do not care:
He, by oath, was pledged;--
And his life, who is forsworn,
That is, ah! so pitiful.

original_japanese:
浅茅生の
小野の篠原
忍ぶれど
あまりてなどか
人の恋しき
original_romaji:
Asajiu no
Ono no shinohara
Shinoburedo
Amarite nado ka
Hito no koishiki
dickens_text_1866:
Like humble Asajiu amid
The reeds of Ono's moor hid,
I would my passion were concealed
But by its flower the Asajiu:
By my too ardent love for you
My secret passion stands revealed.
noguchi_text_1907:
’Tis too much to keep secret. (Oh I would
My heart were unrevealed like that
Of grass-grown One’s bamboo bush!)
Why do I love her so?
porter_text_1909:
’Tis easier to hide the reeds
Upon the moor that grow,
Than try to hide the ardent love
That sets my cheeks aglow
For somebody I know.
maccauley_text_1917:
Bamboo-growing plain,
With a small-field bearing reeds!
Though I bear my lot,
Why is it too much to bear?
Why do I still love her so?

original_japanese:
忍ぶれど
色に出でにけり
わが恋は
物や思ふと
人の問ふまで
original_romaji:
Shinoburedo
Iro ni ide ni keri
Waga koi wa
Mono ya omou to
Hito no tou made
dickens_text_1866:
Tho' aye I strive my lot to hide,
My face to all the secret tells:
My changing visage, sorely tried:
Shows that deep passion in me dwells:
And all men ask
What griefs my altered features task?
noguchi_text_1907:
Alas, my face betrayed
The secret of my love.
All men ask me why
I am so sad.
porter_text_1909:
Alas! the blush upon my cheek,
Conceal it as I may,
Proclaims to all that I'm in love,
Till people smile and say—
'Where are thy thoughts to-day?'
maccauley_text_1917:
Though I would conceal,
In my face it yet appears,--
My fond, secret love:--
So much that he asks of me,
"Does not something trouble you?"

original_japanese:
恋すてふ
我が名はまだき
立ちにけり
人しれずこそ
思ひそめしか
original_romaji:
Koisu cho
Waga na wa madaki
Tachi ni keri
Hito shirezu koso
Omoi someshi ka
dickens_text_1866:
My love for thee of every tongue
The daily theme is--far and wide
My name is bruited men among.
Ah me! my heart was sorely tried
With no unfounded fears, lest
My love to all should stand confest.
noguchi_text_1907:
That I love thee
Is known already. Ah, me!
I had been thinking that
No one would know it.
porter_text_1909:
Our courtship, that we tried to hide,
Misleading is to none;
And yet how could the neighbours guess,
That I had yet begun
To fancy any one?
maccauley_text_1917:
Though, indeed, I love,
Yet, the rumor of my love
Had gone far and wide,
When no man, ere then, could know
That I had begun to love.

original_japanese:
ちぎりきな
かたみに袖を
しぼりつつ
末の松山
波こさじとは
original_romaji:
Chigiriki na
Katami ni sode o
Shibori tsutsu
Sue no Matsuyama
Nami kosaji to wa
dickens_text_1866:
When last each other we embraced,
A solemn vow of faith we swore,
And sealed it with the tears that chased
Adown our cheeks our drench'd sleeves o'er--
That we our oath would fail to keep
When th' waves o'erleapt S'ye's pine-crown'd steep.
noguchi_text_1907:
Didst not thou promise me,
With sleeves full of parting tears, thy heart
Would be safe like Suyeno Matsuyama
Where no billow comes?
porter_text_1909:
Our sleeves, all wet with tears, attest
That you and I agree
That to each other we'll be true,
Till Pine-tree Hill shall be
Sunk far beneath the sea.
maccauley_text_1917:
Have we not been pledged
By the wringing of our sleeves,--
Each for each in turn,--
That o'er Sue's Mount of Pines
Ocean waves shall never pass?

original_japanese:
逢ひ見ての
後の心に
くらぶれば
むかしは物を
思はざりけり
original_romaji:
Ai mite no
Nochi no kokoro ni
Kurabureba
Mukashi wa mono o
Omowazari keri
dickens_text_1866:
I went to meet thee, dearest maid,
And when I parted loth from thee,
Upon my soul such mis'ry weighed,
I mourned the love that burdened me:
O that my heart
Were still unvexed by lover's smart!
noguchi_text_1907:
Oh, to think the sad heart of mine
After meeting with thee!
No sorrow I had
In the olden time.
porter_text_1909:
How desolate my former life,
Those dismal years, ere yet
I chanced to see thee face to face
’Twere better to forget
Those days before we met.
maccauley_text_1917:
Having met my love,
Afterwards my passion was,
When I measured it
With the feeling of the past,
As, if then, I had not loved.

original_japanese:
逢ふことの
絶えてしなくは
中々に
人をも身をも
恨みざらまし
original_romaji:
Au koto no
Taete shi nakuwa
Nakanaka ni
Hito o mo mi o mo
Urami zaramashi
dickens_text_1866:
To love, were it not human fate,
Then men their fellows would not shun,
Their very selves they would not hate,
As since love's birth they've ever done.
noguchi_text_1907:
Oh, if there were no meeting
And loving! I should have
Nothing to resent,
Nothing of myself and others.
porter_text_1909:
To fall in love with womankind
Is my unlucky fate;
If only it were otherwise,
I might appreciate
Some men, whom now I hate.
maccauley_text_1917:
If a trysting time
There should never be at all,
I should not complain
For myself (oft left forlorn),
Or of her (in heartless mood).

original_japanese:
あはれとも
いふべき人は
思ほえで
身のいたづらに
なりぬべきかな
original_romaji:
Aware to mo
Iu beki hito wa
Omooede
Mi no itazura ni
Narinu beki kana
dickens_text_1866:
Ah cruel one! thou pass'dst me by,
No glance of pity on me turned,
A careless soorn was in thine eye,
That mock'd the passion that in me burn'd:
Alas! alas!
Such woes my failing pow're surpass.
noguchi_text_1907:
There’s no one to say
Even a word of pity on me.
Oh my lover lost!
What a misery of my life!
porter_text_1909:
I dare not hope my lady-love
Will smile on me again;
She knows no Pity, and my life
I care not to retain,
Since all my prayers are vain.
maccauley_text_1917:
Sure that there is none
Who will speak a pitying word,
I shall pass away.
Ah! my death shall only be
My own folly's (fitting end).

original_japanese:
由良のとを
わたる舟人
かぢをたえ
行く方もしらぬ
恋の道かな
original_romaji:
Yura no to o
Wataru funabito
Kaji o tae
Yukue mo shiranu
Koi no michi kana
dickens_text_1866:
The fishers' barques in safety glide
O'er th' broad expanse of Yura's bay,
Their rudder lost o'er Yura's tide,
In vague uncertain path they stray:
The course of love doth, too,
A like uncertain path pursue.
noguchi_text_1907:
The boatman of the Yura strait
Lost his rudder, and knows not
How to cross!
Oh the way of love!
porter_text_1909:
The fishing-boats are tossed about,
When stormy winds blow strong;
With rudder lost, how can they reach
The port for which they long?
So runs the old love-song.
maccauley_text_1917:
Like a mariner
Sailing over Yura's strait
With his rudder gone,--
Whither, o'er the deep of love,
Lies the goal, I do not know.

original_japanese:
八重むぐら
しげれる宿の
さびしきに
人こそ見えね
秋は来にけり
original_romaji:
Yaemugura
Shigereru yado no
Sabishiki ni
Hito koso miene
Aki wa ki ni keri
dickens_text_1866:
My mountain dwelling's rood of thatch
Is with Yahemugura moss o'ergrown,
Of passer-by no glimpse I catch,
I dwell uncheered and alone;
'Tis autumn time,
And mandkind dread the rig'rous clime.
noguchi_text_1907:
My hut with Yaemugura
Thickly grown is sad:
Here nobody will be seen,
But Autumn has come.
porter_text_1909:
My little temple stands alone,
No other hut is near;
No one will pass to stop and praise
Its vine-grown roof, I fear,
Now that the autumn's here.
maccauley_text_1917:
To the humble cot,
Overgrown with thick-leaved vines
In its loneliness,
Comes the dreary autumn time;--
And not even man is there.

original_japanese:
風をいたみ
岩うつ波の
おのれのみ
くだけて物を
おもふ頃かな
original_romaji:
Kaze o itami
Iwa utsu nami no
Onore nomi
Kudakete mono o
Omou koro kana
dickens_text_1866:
From th' pitiless rock are backwards flung
The wind urged floods in scattered spary.
With prayers from anguished heart-depths wrung,
I seek to make thee, love, obey;
As spurns the rock
The waves, dost thou my passion mock.
noguchi_text_1907:
A crushed wave I am
Against the rock, in storm:
Oh, these days!
What a lonely thought of mine!
porter_text_1909:
The waves that dash against the rocks
Are broken by the wind
And turned to spray; my loving heart
Is broken too, I find,
Since thou art so unkind.
maccauley_text_1917:
Like a driven wave,
Dashed by fierce winds on a rock,
So it is, alas!
Crushed and all alone am I;
Thinking over what has been.

original_japanese:
みかき守
衛士のたく火の
夜はもえ
昼は消えつつ
物をこそおもへ
original_romaji:
Mikakimori
Eji no taku hi no
Yoru wa moe
Hiru wa kie tsutsu
Mono o koso omoe
dickens_text_1866:
The' Mikaki-mori through the night
(And men the warder Yeji name)
The watch-fire's blaze keeps full and bright;
When morning breaks, then dies the flame:
So, too, at dawn
My happiness is past and gone.
noguchi_text_1907:
Through the night the Mikakimori guards
Burn the fire: Oh, my heart!
But the fire will die in day:
Oh, my dying thought!
porter_text_1909:
My constancy to her I love
I never will forsake;
As surely as the Palace Guards
Each night their watch-fire make
And guard it till daybreak.
maccauley_text_1917:
Like the warder's fires
At the Imperial gateway kept,--
Burning through the night,
Through the day in ashes dulled,--
Is the love aglow in me.

original_japanese:
君がため
惜しからざりし
命さへ
ながくもがなと
おもひけるかな
original_romaji:
Kimi ga tame
Oshi karazarishi
Inochi sae
Nagaku mo gana to
Omoi keru kana
dickens_text_1866:
Ere I, O maid! had worshipped thee,
A drear uncared-for life was mine:---
O may long years be granted me
Now that my heart, O maid, is thine!
noguchi_text_1907:
For thee, I thought,
I would not mind about my life:
But I pray now to be
Given the longest life.
porter_text_1909:
Death had no terrors, Life no joys,
Before I met with thee;
But now I fear, however long
My life may chance to be,
’Twill be too short for me!
maccauley_text_1917:
For thy precious sake,
Once my (eager) life itself
Was not dear to me.
But 'tis now my heart's desire
It may long, long years endure.

original_japanese:
かくとだに
えやはいぶきの
さしも草
さしも知らじな
もゆる思ひを
original_romaji:
Kaku to dani
Eyawa ibuki no
Sashimogusa
Sashimo shiraji na
Moyuru omoi o
dickens_text_1866:
To tell thee of my love were vain,
Its depth to me is scarcely known:
As writhes the flesh 'neath Moxa's pain,
The moxa on Ibuki grown,
So madly writhes my spirit 'mong
Love's flames, ere now unknown, sore wrung.
noguchi_text_1907:
How could I tell thee
My burning heart?
(Ah, my heart burning as under
An Ibuki Moxa’s sting!).
porter_text_1909:
Though love, like blisters made from leaves
Grown on Mount Ibuki,
Torments me more than I can say,
My lady shall not see,
How she is paining me.
maccauley_text_1917:
That, 'tis as it is,
How can I make known to her?
So, she may n'er know
That the love I feel for her
Like Ibuki's moxa burns.

original_japanese:
明けぬれば
暮るるものとは
知りながら
なをうらめしき
あさぼらけかな
original_romaji:
Akenureba
Kururu mono to wa
Shiri nagara
Nao urameshiki
Asaborake kana
dickens_text_1866:
When day breaks, tho' full well I know
The darkness of the ensuing night
The hated day shall overthrow:
Yet aye the daylight I do hate,
And bitterly mourn
Th' unwelcome breaking of the dawn.
noguchi_text_1907:
Day will be followed by
The darkness of night when I shall meet thee,
And yet I do hate
The breaking of dawn.
porter_text_1909:
Although I know the gentle night
Will surely follow morn,
Yet, when I'm wakened by the sun,
Turn over, stretch and yawn—
How I detest the dawn!
maccauley_text_1917:
Though I know full well
That the night will come again
E'en when day has dawned,
Yet, in truth, I hate the sight
Of the morning's coming light.

original_japanese:
なげきつつ
ひとりぬる夜の
明くる間は
いかに久しき
ものとかは知る
original_romaji:
Nageki tsutsu
Hitori nuru yo no
Akuru ma wa
Ikani hisashiki
Mono to ka wa shiru
dickens_text_1866:
I have watched weeping through the night,
Deserted, desolate, alone
Till now hath broke the morning light
I almost deemed for ever gone,
So slowly by
The creeping hours seemed to hie.
noguchi_text_1907:
What a long time
To the dawn
When I weep through the night,
And sleep alone!
porter_text_1909:
All through the long and dreary night
I lie awake and moan;
How desolate my chamber feels,
How weary I have grown
Of being left alone!
maccauley_text_1917:
Sighing all alone,
Through the long watch of the night,
Till the break of day:--
Can you realize at all
What a tedious thing it is?

original_japanese:
忘れじの
行末までは
難ければ
今日を限りの
命ともがな
original_romaji:
Wasureji no
Yukusue made wa
Katakereba
Kyo o kagiri no
Inochi to mo gana
dickens_text_1866:
To keep the vows that lovers swear
Of faithfulness and constancy
Through life till death end worldly care,
O'ertasketh human frailty,
I trow. To-day
I'd fain my spirit fled away.
noguchi_text_1907:
To vow for the future long
With faith and unforgetfulness would be
Too hard. Oh, I pray,
To-day, to have my life done!
porter_text_1909:
How difficult it is for men
Not to forget the past!
I fear my husband's love for me
Is disappearing fast;
This day must be my last.
maccauley_text_1917:
If "not to forget"
Will for him in future years
Be too difficult;--
It were well this very day
That my life, ah me! should close.

original_japanese:
滝の音は
絶えて久しく
なりぬれど
名こそ流れて
なほ聞えけれ
original_romaji:
Taki no oto wa
Taete hisashiku
Narinuredo
Na koso nagarete
Nao kikoe kere
dickens_text_1866:
The noisy play of the waterfall
Hath ceased long ago,
Yet aye shall men its fame recall,
Tho' none now list its flow.
noguchi_text_1907:
’Tis long time now since.
The waterfall ceased its voice,
But the fame does run,
And is to be heard still.
porter_text_1909:
This waterfall's melodious voice
Was famed both far and near;
Although it long has ceased to flow,
Yet still with memory's ear
Its gentle splash I hear.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though the waterfall
In its flow ceased long ago,
And its sound is stilled;
Yet, in name it ever flows,
And in fame may yet be heard.

original_japanese:
あらざらむ
この世の外の
思ひ出に
今ひとたびの
逢ふこともがな
original_romaji:
Arazaran
Kono yo no hoka no
Omoide ni
Ima hitotabi no
Au koto mo gana
dickens_text_1866:
Ere long for me this world shall end,
Thus doth my mind to me foretell;
Ere long to other world shall wend
My soul that thee hath lov'd so well.
Ah! would that thou
But once more wer't beside me now.
noguchi_text_1907:
Who knows when I shall die!
Oh, for pity’s sake,
I pray to see thee
Once more!
porter_text_1909:
My life is drawing to a close,
I cannot longer stay,
A pleasant memory of thee
I fain would take away;
So visit me, I pray.
maccauley_text_1917:
Soon I cease to be;--
One fond memory I would keep
When beyond this world.
Is there, then, no way for me
Just once more to meet with thee?

original_japanese:
めぐりあひて
見しやそれとも
わかぬ間に
雲がくれにし
夜半の月かげ
original_romaji:
Meguri aite
Mishi ya sore to mo
Wakanu ma ni
Kumo-gakure ni shi
Yowa no tsuki kage
dickens_text_1866:
I ventured forth one moonlight night,
And then saw some one hastening past,
Ere I could tell who 'twas aright,
With dark clouds was the moon o'ercast
Whose pallid ray
O'er the middle night held tranquil sway.
noguchi_text_1907:
I met him by chance
And I parted from him ere I could tell
Who he was. Alas, passed in the cloud
The midnight moon!
porter_text_1909:
I wandered forth this moonlight night,
And some one hurried by;
But who it was I could not see,—
Clouds driving o'er the sky
Obscured the moon on high..
maccauley_text_1917:
Meeting in the way--,
While I can not clearly know
If 'tis friend or not;--
Lo! the midnight moon, ah me!
In a cloud has disappeared.

original_japanese:
ありま山
猪名の笹原
風吹けば
いでそよ人を
忘れやはする
original_romaji:
Arimayama
Ina no sasawara
Kaze fukeba
Ide soyo hito o
Wasure ya wa suru
dickens_text_1866:
More fickle thou than th' winds that pout
Down Arima o'er Ina's moor,
And still my love for thee as yet
I have forgotten to forget.
noguchi_text_1907:
(The wind may blow
From Arima Hill and Inano bamboo bush.)
Ah, passing wind of thy love!
But how could one forget thee!
porter_text_1909:
As fickle as the mountain gusts
That on the moor I've met,
’Twere best to think no more of thee,
And let thee go. But yet
I never can forget.
maccauley_text_1917:
If Mount Arima
Sends his rustling winds across
Ina's bamboo-plains;--
Well! in truth, tis as you say;
Yet how can I e'er forget?

original_japanese:
やすらはで
寝なまし物を
小夜更けて
かたぶくまでの
月を見しかな
original_romaji:
Yasurawade
Nenamashi mono o
Sayo fukete
Katabuku made no
Tsuki o mishi kana
dickens_text_1866:
I wait thy coming, love--repose
Veils not mine eyes--far in the night
I watch the moon till nigh the close
Of her celestial path of light.
noguchi_text_1907:
I should not wait for him,
But go to sleep. Alas, I have been gazing
Upon the moon in deep night
Till she begins to fall.
porter_text_1909:
Waiting and hoping for thy step,
Sleepless in bed I lie,
All through the night, until the moon,
Leaving her post on high,
Slips sideways down the sky.
maccauley_text_1917:
Better to have slept
Care-free, than to keep vain watch
Through the passing night,
Till I saw the lonely moon.
Traverse her descending path.

original_japanese:
大江山
いく野の道の
とほければ
まだふみも見ず
天の橋立
original_romaji:
Oeyama
Ikuno no michi no
To kereba
Mada fumi mo mizu
Ama no Hashidate
dickens_text_1866:
The road the crosseth o'er the plain
Towards Ikuno's full long for thee,
The road that far away doth gain
The distant range of Ohoye:
At Ama-no-hashi-date e'en
Thy footsteps yet yath no one seen.
noguchi_text_1907:
’Tis far away to Ohoye mountain,
And to Ikuno plain. I have never stepped
In Ama no Hashidate yet.
(Alas, no letter I have seen!)
porter_text_1909:
So long and dreary is the road,
That I have never been
To Ama-no-Hashidate;
Pray, how could I have seen
The verses that you mean?
maccauley_text_1917:
As, by Oe's mount
And o'er Iku's plain, the way
Is so very far,--
I have not yet even seen
Ama-no-hashidate.

original_japanese:
いにしへの
奈良の都の
八重桜
今日九重に
匂ひぬるかな
original_romaji:
Inishie no
Nara no miyako no
Yae-zakura
Kyo kokonoe ni
Nioi nuru kana
dickens_text_1866:
Of old the Yahezak'ra lent
To Nara, capital of yore,
Its fragrancy, and now its scent
Hath spread our Kokonohe o'er
noguchi_text_1907:
’Tis the eight-holded cherry blossom
Of Nara capital of yore:
To-day in this nine-folded palace
It will shed its perfume.
porter_text_1909:
The double cherry trees, which grew
At Nara in past days,
Now beautify this Palace, and
Their blossoms all ablaze
Perfume the royal ways.
maccauley_text_1917:
Eight-fold cherry flowers
That at Nara,--ancient seat
Of Our State,--have bloomed;--
In Our Nine-fold Palace court
Shed their sweet perfume today

original_japanese:
夜をこめて
鳥の空音は
はかるとも
よにあふさかの
関はゆるさじ
original_romaji:
Yo o komete
Tori no sorane wa
Hakaru tomo
Yo ni Osaka no
Seki wa yurusaji
dickens_text_1866:
Tho' thou, the guardians of the gate
Of Kan-kok'-kan, with false cock-crow,
Might'st cheat, and thus anticipate
The morn, thou ne'er canst cheat, I trow,
Ausaka's gate, that thee
Shall keep until the morning be.
noguchi_text_1907:
Thou might’st try to cheat me,
With the false voice of a bird,
But the Ausaka gate
Shall not allow thee in
porter_text_1909:
Too long to-night you've lingered here,
And, though you imitate
The crowing of a cock, 'twill not
Unlock the tollbar gate;
Till daylight must you wait.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though in middle night,
By the feigned crow of the cock,
Some may be deceived;--
Yet, at Ausaka's gate
This can never be achieved.

original_japanese:
今はただ
思ひ絶えなむ
とばかりを
人づてならで
いふよしもがな
original_romaji:
Ima wa tada
Omoi taenan
To bakari wo
Hito-zute nara de
Iu yoshi mo gana
dickens_text_1866:
Now doth deep misery oppress
My vex'd and sorrow'd mind
To none will I my woe confess,
Save thee, among mankind:
With thee I seek
Of all my wretchedness to speak.
noguchi_text_1907:
Alas, there’s no way
But to ask one to tell thee
That we will try
To forget.
porter_text_1909:
If we could meet in privacy,
Where no one else could see,
Softly I'd whisper in thy ear
This little word from me—
'I'm dying, Love, for thee.'
maccauley_text_1917:
Is there now no way,
But through others' lips, to say
These so fateful words,--
That, henceforth, my love for you
I must banish from my thoughts?

original_japanese:
朝ぼらけ
宇治の川ぎり
たえだえに
あらはれわたる
ぜぜの網代木
original_romaji:
Asaborake
Uji no kawagiri
Tae-dae ni
Araware wataru
Zeze no ajirogi
dickens_text_1866:
By th' dim grey light of early dawn
I stray'd by Uji's wave,
From whence the rifting mist upborne
Me scattered glimpses gave
Of Zeze's stakes there set,
Whereon the fisher spreads his net.
noguchi_text_1907:
From amid the Uji river the mists fade
At early morn,
The fisher’s net stakes begin
To appear, here and there.
porter_text_1909:
So thickly lies the morning mist,
That I can scarcely see
The fish-nets on the river bank,
The River of Uji,
Past daybreak though it be.
maccauley_text_1917:
Lo! at early dawn,
When the mists o'er Uji's stream
Slowly lift and clear,
And the net-stakes on the shoals,
Near and far away, appear!

original_japanese:
恨みわび
ほさぬ袖だに
あるものを
恋に朽ちなん
名こそ惜しけれ
original_romaji:
Urami wabi
Hosanu sode da ni
Aru mono o
Koi ni kuchinan
Na koso oshi kere
dickens_text_1866:
Despised, I weep thy long neglect,
My tears drench my sleeve,
The happiness of my life is wrecked
In struggles to achieve
Thy stubborn love:
My fate might all men's pity move.
noguchi_text_1907:
From my resentment, in tears
My sleeves are drenched.
What a shame to ruin my name
In such an empty love!
porter_text_1909:
Be not displeased, but pardon me,
If still my tears o’erflow;
My lover's gone, and my good name,
Which once I valued so,
I fear must also go.
maccauley_text_1917:
Even when my sleeves,
Through my hate and misery,
Never once are dry,--
For such love my name decays:--
How deplorable my lot!

original_japanese:
もろともに
哀れと思へ
山桜
花より外に
知る人もなし
original_romaji:
Morotomo ni
Aware to omoe
Yama-zakura
Hana yori hoka ni
Shiru hito mo nashi
dickens_text_1866:
With thee, O mountain Sakura tree!
A lonely fate I moan,
Thy blossom only cheers me--
The only friend I own.
noguchi_text_1907:
Be sad with me,
Oh, mountain cherry blossom!
I have no one
Knows my heart but thee
maccauley_text_1917:
Let us, each for each
Pitying, hold tender thought,
Mountain-cherry flower!
Other than thee, lonely flower,
There is none I know as friend.

original_japanese:
春の夜の
夢ばかりなる
手枕に
かひなく立たむ
名こそ惜しけれ
original_romaji:
Haru no yo no
Yume bakari naru
Tamakura ni
Kainaku tatan
Na koso oshi kere
dickens_text_1866:
Had I made thy proffer'd arm
A pillow for my wearied head,
No longer e'en than lasts the charm
Of a spring-night's dream--what had rumour said?
How would my fame
Have suffer'd from men's sland'ring blame!
noguchi_text_1907:
For a short while,—short
Like a Spring night dream, in taking
Thy arm for my pillow, what a shame
To have a bad rumor rise!
porter_text_1909:
If I had made thy proffered arm
A pillow for my head
For but the moment's time, in which
A summer's dream had fled,
What would the world have said?
maccauley_text_1917:
If, but through the dreams
Of a spring's short night, I'd rest
Pillowed on this arm,
And my name were blameless stained,
Hard, indeed, would be my fate.

original_japanese:
心にも
あらで浮世に
ながらへば
恋しかるべき
夜半の月かな
original_romaji:
Kokoro ni mo
Arade ukiyo ni
Nagaraeba
Koishikaru beki
Yowa no tsuki kana
dickens_text_1866:
Fain would I in this world so hard
No longer live, but still must stay:--
How wistfully my eyes regards
The midnight moonbeams' tranquil sway!
noguchi_text_1907:
In spite of myself, I am
Lingering in this world:
Ah, what longing
For the midnight moon!
porter_text_1909:
If in this troubled world of ours
I still must linger on,
My only friend shall be the moon,
Which on my sadness shone,
When other friends were gone.
maccauley_text_1917:
If, against my wish,
In the world of sorrows still,
I for long should live;--
How then I would pine, alas!
For this moon of middle-night.

original_japanese:
あらし吹く
三室の山の
もみぢ葉は
龍田の川の
にしきなりけり
original_romaji:
Arashi fuku
Mimuro no yama no
Momijiba wa
Tatsuta no kawa no
Nishiki nari keri
dickens_text_1866:
Round Mimuro-yama lustily
The storm-winds roar and whirl,
And th' scatter'd leaves of th' momiji
In the reddening Tatsta hurl.
noguchi_text_1907:
The Mimuro Mountain maple leaves
In blowing storm,
Weave the blockade
For the Tatsuda stream.
porter_text_1909:
The storms, which round Mount Mimuro
Are wont to howl and scream,
Have thickly scattered maple leaves
Upon Tatsuta's stream;
Like red brocade they seem.
maccauley_text_1917:
By the wind-storm's blast,
From Mimuro's mountain slopes
Maples leaves are torn,
And as (rich) brocades, are wrought
On (blue) Tatta's (quiet) stream.

original_japanese:
寂しさに
宿を立出て
ながむれば
いづこもおなじ
秋の夕暮
original_romaji:
Sabishisa ni
Yado o tachi idete
Nagamureba
Izuko mo onaji
Aki no yugure
dickens_text_1866:
In lonely solitude my home,
And from my cabin when I stray,
Where'er my wan'ring eyes may roam,
The landscape that doth round me lay,
How desolate, how drear
Doth it at autumn-e'en appear.
noguchi_text_1907:
From loneliness I wander
Out of my own home:
Lo, ’tis the same everywhere
This Autumn eve!
porter_text_1909:
The prospect from my cottage shows
No other hut in sight;
The solitude depresses me,
Like deepening twilight
On a chill autumn night.
maccauley_text_1917:
In my loneliness
From my humble home gone forth,
When I looked around,
Everywhere it was the same;--
One lone, darkening autumn eve.

original_japanese:
夕されば
門田の稲葉
おとづれて
あしのまろやに
秋風ぞふく
original_romaji:
Yu sareba
Kadota no inaba
Otozurete
Ashi no maroya ni
Akikaze zo fuku
dickens_text_1866:
Now twilight darkens, and the breeze
Rustles the homeside rice-fields 'mong,
And murmuring sounds my ear please,
As past my hut with thatch o'erhung
Of Ashi grass,
The sweeping gusts of autumn pass.
noguchi_text_1907:
At eve,
By the ashi grass hut,
The Autumn gusts pass, calling on
The gate-side rice plant leaves.
porter_text_1909:
This autumn night the wind blows shrill,
And would that I could catch
Its message, as it whistles through
The rushes in the thatch
And leaves of my rice-patch.
maccauley_text_1917:
When the evening comes,
From the rice leaves at my gate
Gentle knocks are heard;
And, into my round rush-hut,
Autumn's roaming breeze makes way.

original_japanese:
音にきく
高師の浜の
あだ浪は
かけじや袖の
ぬれもこそすれ
original_romaji:
Oto ni kiku
Takashi no hama no
Adanami wa
Kakeji ya sode no
Nure mo koso sure
dickens_text_1866:
Thy beauty is throughout the land
As well-known as the furious play
Of billow on Takashi's strand,
That drench the venturesome with spray,
Who come their sweep too nigh:
So she who hath thee once beheld,
To tears of jealous love compelled,
Her sleeve shall ne'er be dry.
noguchi_text_1907:
’Tis known to the world,
Ah me, the fickle waves
Of the Takashi strand do drench
One’s sleeves with spray.
porter_text_1909:
The sound of ripples on the shore
Ne’er fails at Takashi;
My sleeves all worn and wet with tears
Should surely prove to thee,
I, too, will constant be.
maccauley_text_1917:
Well I know the fame
Of the fickle waves that beat
On Takashi's strand!
Should I e'er go near that shore
I should only wet my sleeves.

original_japanese:
高砂の
尾の上の桜
咲きにけり
外山の霞
たたずもあらなん
original_romaji:
Takasago no
Onoe no sakura
Saki ni keri
Toyama no kasumi
Tatazu mo aranan
dickens_text_1866:
The Sakura trees in plenty grow
On Takasago's steep hill-side,
And now their crowded blossoms show;
O may no fogs their beauty hide,
No mists from hill-top rise
To veil their radiance from our eyes.
noguchi_text_1907:
On Takasago Mountain
The cherry trees are blossoming:
The mists from the other hills
Shall not rise, I pray.
porter_text_1909:
The cherry trees are blossoming
On Takasago's height;
Oh may no mountain mist arise,
No clouds so soft and white,
To hide them from our sight.
maccauley_text_1917:
On that distant mount,
O'er the slope below the peak,
Cherries are in flower;--
May the mists of hither hills
Not arise to veil the scene.

original_japanese:
うかりける
人をはつせの
山おろしよ
はげしかれとは
祈らぬものを
original_romaji:
Ukari keru
Hito o Hatsuse no
Yama oroshiyo
Hageshikare to wa
Inoranu mono o
dickens_text_1866:
As windy blasts down Hasse's steep
In furious path impetuous sweep,
So rudely thou my suit dost slight,
And scorn thy lover's hapless plight;
No more 'fore Hasse's shrine
Will I in suing prayer incline.
noguchi_text_1907:
Oh, did I pray
The Hatsuse mountain blast,
Nay, his heartlessness, to be furious?
Nay, I did not!
porter_text_1909:
Oh! Kwannon, Patron of this hill,
The maid, for whom I pine,
Is obstinate and wayward, like
The gusts around thy shrine.
What of those prayers of mine?
maccauley_text_1917:
I did not make prayer
(At the shrine of Mercy's God),
That the unkind one
Should become as pitiless
As the storms of Hase's hills.

original_japanese:
契りをきし
させもが露を
命にて
あはれことしの
秋もいぬめり
original_romaji:
Chigiri okishi
Sasemo ga tsuyu o
Inochi ni te
Aware kotoshi no
Aki mo inumeri
dickens_text_1866:
A covenant thou mad'st with me,
And as the Sasemo from th' dew,
So I my very life from thee
Drink in. Alas! I fear me
This autumn's days are now but few!
noguchi_text_1907:
The sasaemo's life is a dew
Ah me! Where’s thy promise?
Autumn of this year
Is passing away.
porter_text_1909:
It is a promise unfulfilled,
For which I humbly sue
The dainty little mugwort plant
Relies upon the dew,
And I rely—on you.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though your promise was
"Like the dew on moxa plant"
And, to me, was life;
Yet, alas! the year has passed
Even into autumn time.

original_japanese:
わたの原
こぎ出でて見れば
久方の
雲井にまよふ
おきつしらなみ
original_romaji:
Wata no hara
Kogi idete mireba
Hisakata no
Kumoi ni mayoo
Okitsu shiranami
dickens_text_1866:
In fisher's barque I onward glide
O'er th' broad expanse of ocean's tide,
And towards th' horizons when I turn
My glance I scarcely can discern
Where the white-tipped billows end,
That with the cloud-horizon blend.
noguchi_text_1907:
Over the expanse of sea I row.
Behold the far-away sky,
Nay, the billows white
In the distance!
porter_text_1909:
When rowing on the open sea,
The waves, all capped with white,
Roll onward, like the fleecy clouds
With their resistless might;
Truly a wondrous sight!
maccauley_text_1917:
O'er the wide sea plain,
As I row and look around,
It appears to me
That the white waves, far away,
Are the ever shining sky.

original_japanese:
瀬をはやみ
岩にせかるる
滝川の
われても末に
逢はむとぞ思ふ
original_romaji:
Se o hayami
Iwa ni sekaruru
Takigawa no
Warete mo sue ni
Awan to zo omou
dickens_text_1866:
The brawling strem against the rock
Its tumbling waters fiercely hurls,
Divided by the furious shock,
In double torret onwards whirls:
In further flow
I trow a single stream 'twill show.
noguchi_text_1907:
Like a hurrying, rock-hurling mountain stream
I wish to be: its double torrents
Will meet in the end.
Oh the way of love!
porter_text_1909:
The rock divides the stream in two,
And both with might and main
Go tumbling down the waterfall;
But well I know the twain
Will soon unite again.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though a swift stream be
By a rock met and restrained
In impetuous flow,
Yet, divided, it speeds on,
And at last unites again.

original_japanese:
淡路島
かよふ千鳥の
なく声に
いくよねざめぬ
すまの関守
original_romaji:
Awaji shima
Kayou chidori no
Naku koe ni
Ikuyo nezamenu
Suma no sekimori
dickens_text_1866:
'Tween Awaji and Suma fly
The screaming sea-birds to and fro
Night after night; their ceaseless cry
Doth scarce a moment's sleep allow,
To whom his fate
Allots the ward of Suma's gate.
noguchi_text_1907:
By the cry of the plovers
That frequent Awazi Isle,
How many nights art thou awakened,
Guard of the Suma gate?
porter_text_1909:
Between Awaji and the shore
The birds scream in their flight
Full oft they've made the Suma Guard
Toss through a sleepless night,
Until the morning light.
maccauley_text_1917:
Guard of Suma's Gate,
From your sleep, how many nights
Have you waked at cries
Of the plaintive sanderlings,
Migrant from Awaji's isle?

original_japanese:
秋風に
たなびく雲の
たえまより
もれ出づる月の
かげのさやけさ
original_romaji:
Akikaze ni
Tanabiku kumo no
Taema yori
More izuru tsuki no
Kage no sayakesa
dickens_text_1866:
When bloweth autumn's chilly blast,
Through rifts at times the moonbeams peep,
From 'mid the dark clouds drifting past,
And earth in pallid radiance steep,
I love to see
The bright-edged shadows o'er the lea.
noguchi_text_1907:
From the rifts of the clouds
Drifting abroad in the Autumn wind,
What a clear shadow
Of the peeping moon!
porter_text_1909:
See how the wind of autumn drives
The clouds to left and right,
While in between the moon peeps out,
Dispersing with her light
The darkness of the night.
maccauley_text_1917:
See, how clear and bright
Is the moon-light finding ways
'Mong the riven clouds
That, with drifting autumn-wind,
Gracefully float o'er the sky!

original_japanese:
長からむ
心もしらず
黒髪の
みだれてけさは
物をこそ思へ
original_romaji:
Nagakaran
Kokoro mo shirazu
Kurokami no
Midarete kesa wa
Mono o koso omoe
dickens_text_1866:
I fear me thou wilt break the pact
Thou mad'st with me--thy love will pass
Away from me, whom thought distract,
As tangled as the unkempt mass
My raven tresses show,
That o'er my waking pillow flow.
noguchi_text_1907:
My heart, I pray,
To last long. Ah, this tangle
of the black tresses of mine!
Ah, my anxiety of this morn!
porter_text_1909:
My doubt about his constancy
Is difficult to bear;
Tangled this morning are my thoughts,
As is my long black hair.
I wonder—Does he care?
maccauley_text_1917:
If it be for aye
That he wills our love should last?
Ah! I do not know!
And this morn my anxious thoughts,
Like my black hair, are confused.

original_japanese:
ほととぎす
鳴きつる方を
眺むれば
ただ有明の
月ぞのこれる
original_romaji:
Hototogisu
Nakitsuru kata o
Nagamureba
Tada ariake no
Tsuki zo nokoreru
dickens_text_1866:
I heard the Hototogis cry,
I searched throughout the echoing sky,
No Hototogis could espy,
The morning moon but met my eye.
noguchi_text_1907:
Behold
The sky where the cuckoo sung!
There remains
Only the morning moon.
porter_text_1909:
The cuckoo's echo dies away,
And lo! the branch is bare
I only see the morning moon,
Whose light is fading there
Before the daylight's glare.
maccauley_text_1917:
When I turned my look
Toward the place whence I had heard
Hototogisu,--
Lo! the only object there
Was the moon of early dawn.

original_japanese:
思ひわび
さても命は
あるものを
憂きに堪へぬは
なみだなりけり
original_romaji:
Omoi wabi
Satemo inochi wa
Aru mono o
Uki ni taenu wa
Namida nari keri
dickens_text_1866:
What wretchedness is mine, O Life!
With what deep mis'ry thou'rt opprest!
With my sad lot I strive in strife
That leaveth me nor peace nor rest;
The tears that flow
Down o'er my cheek my anguish show.
noguchi_text_1907:
And I have my life still
Under wretchedness of thought,
But my own tears alone
Under sadness cannot stand.
porter_text_1909:
How sad and gloomy is the world,
This world of sin and woe!
Ah! while I drift along Life's stream,
Tossed helpless to and fro,
My tears will ever flow.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though in deep distress
(Through the cruel blow), my life
Still is left to me:--
But my tears I can not keep;
They can not my grief endure.

original_japanese:
世の中よ
道こそなけれ
思ひ入る
山のおくにも
鹿ぞ鳴くなる
original_romaji:
Yo no naka yo
Michi koso nakere
Omoi iru
Yama no oku ni mo
Shika zo naku naru
dickens_text_1866:
O'er th' world doth evil aye hold sway
I deemed, and far I fled away
Amis the hills:
But there the deer's sad cry, too, thrills.
noguchi_text_1907:
Alas, ’tis the world;
There’s no way to follow,
Even into the deep of a hill
The deer’s cry I hear.
porter_text_1909:
From pain and sorrow all around
There 's no escape, I fear;
To mountain wilds should I retreat,
There also I should hear
The cry of hunted deer.
maccauley_text_1917:
Ah! within the world,
Way of flight I find nowhere.
I had thought to hide
In the mountains' farthest depths;
Yet e'en there the stag's cry sounds.

original_japanese:
ながらへば
またこの頃や
しのばれむ
憂しと見し世ぞ
今は恋しき
original_romaji:
Nagaraeba
Mata konogoro ya
Shinobaren
Ushi to mishi yo zo
Ima wa koishiki
dickens_text_1866:
Were I to linger more in life,
What seemed of old a grievous strife
Would seem to be a burden slight,
To be borne almost with delight.
noguchi_text_1907:
Were I to linger longer in life,
The present days would grow dear again:
Oh, now I long for
The days I deemed sad in past.
porter_text_1909:
Time was when I despised my youth,
As boyhood only can;
What would I give for boyhood now,
When finishing life's span
An old decrepid man!
maccauley_text_1917:
If I long should live,
Then, perchance, the present days
May be dear to me;--
Just as past time fraught with grief
Now comes fondly back in thought.

original_japanese:
夜もすがら
物思ふ頃は
明けやらぬ
ねやのひまさへ
つれなかりけり
original_romaji:
Yo mo sugara
Mono omou koro wa
Ake yaranu
Neya no hima sae
Tsure nakari keri
dickens_text_1866:
With wretched thoughts distracted I
On sleepless pallet restless lay
The livelong night: with wistful eye
I waited for the breaking day
Through chink of screen
That guards my chamber--peeping, seen.
noguchi_text_1907:
All the night long I thought
It will never dawn:
Even the chink of my chamber door
Is heartless to me, not inviting the morn
porter_text_1909:
All through the never-ending night
I lie awake and think;
In vain I look to try and see
The daybreak's feeble blink
Peep through the shutter's chink.
maccauley_text_1917:
Now,-- as through the night
Longingly I pass the hours,
And the day's dawn lags,--
E'en my bedroom's crannied doors
Heartless are, indeed, to me.

original_japanese:
なげけとて
月やは物を
思はする
かこちがほなる
わがなみだかな
original_romaji:
Nageke tote
Tsuki ya wa mono o
Omowasuru
Kakochi gao naru
Waga namida kana
dickens_text_1866:
With deeper melancholy sways
The moonlight night my love-sick soul;
See how my face my woe betrays,
How down my cheek the tears roll.
noguchi_text_1907:
The moon has nothing to make
Me think and cry,
But, alas, my own tears alone
Do lament and fall.
porter_text_1909:
O'ercome with pity for this world,
My tears obscure my sight;
I wonder, can it be the moon
Whose melancholy light
Has saddened me to-night?
maccauley_text_1917:
Is it then the moon
That has made me sad, as though
It had bade me grieve?
Lifting up my troubled face,--
Ah! the tears, the (mournful) tears!

original_japanese:
むらさめの
露もまだひぬ
まきの葉に
霧立ちのぼる
秋の夕暮
original_romaji:
Murasame no
Tsuyu mo mada hinu
Maki no ha ni
Kiri tachinoboru
Aki no yugure
dickens_text_1866:
The passing shower onwards sweeps,--
Not yet upon the yew-leaves dried
Its scattered drops,--and lo! there creeps
The rising mist up yon hill-side
Of autumn e'en
At twilight's chilly hour seen.
noguchi_text_1907:
The dews of the passing shower
Are not yet dried.
Lo, the mist rising up
Toward the maki leaves, this Autumn eve!
porter_text_1909:
The rain, which fell from passing showers,
Like drops of dew, still lies
Upon the fir-tree needles, and
The mists of evening rise
Up to the autumn skies.
maccauley_text_1917:
Lo, an autumn eve!
See the deep vale's mists arise
Mong the fir-tree's leaves
That still hold the dripping wet
Of the (chill day's) sudden showers.

original_japanese:
難波江の
芦のかりねの
一夜ゆへ
身をつくしてや
恋わたるべき
original_romaji:
Naniwae no
Ashi no karine no
Hitoyo yue
Mi o tsukushite ya
Koi wataru beki
dickens_text_1866: The plans upon words in this Ode render it quite untranslateable, with any approach, at all events, to the force and point of the original. I have subjoined an explanation of it in the Appendix
noguchi_text_1907:
’Twas a short one night love
At the Niniwa shore. (Short ’twas
Like a joint of the shore reed.)
Why do I long, exhausting me so?
maccauley_text_1917:
For but one night's sake,
Short as is a node of reed
Grown in Naniwa bay,
Must I, henceforth, long for him
With my whole heart, till life's close?

original_japanese:
玉の緒よ
絶えなば絶えね
ながらへば
しのぶることの
よはりもぞする
original_romaji:
Tama no o yo
Taenaba taene
Nagaraeba
Shinoburu koto no
Yowari mo zo suru
dickens_text_1866:
Of my life or soon or late the thread,
The withering threat perforce must snap:
I almost would 'twere now, I dread
Of longer life the sure hap--
The secret of our love displayed,
For e'er our happiness low laid.
noguchi_text_1907:
Oh, thread of my life,
Be torn off now if it must!
I fear in longer life
My secret would be hard to keep.
porter_text_1909:
The ailments of advancing years
Though I should try to hide,
Some day the thread will break, the pearls
Be scattered far and wide;
Age cannot be defied.
maccauley_text_1917:
Life! Thou string of gems!
If thou art to end, break now.
For, if yet I live,
All I do to hide ( my love)
May at last grow weak (and fail).

original_japanese:
見せばやな
雄島のあまの
袖だにも
ぬれにぞぬれし
色はかはらず
original_romaji:
Misebaya na
Ojima no ama no
Sode dani mo
Nure ni zo nureshi
Iro wa kawarazu
dickens_text_1866:
I would that I might show to thee
The island-fisher's oft-drenched sleeve,
I would that thine own eyes might see
How the salt waves their tints ne'er thieve;
From mine, alas!
Aye tear-bedewed, the colours pass.
noguchi_text_1907:
I might show thee
How the Oshima island fishers’ sleeves
Never change their tints, though wet through.
But, alas, tearful sleeves of mine!
porter_text_1909:
The fisher's clothes, though cheap, withstand
The drenching they receive;
But see I my floods of tears have blurred
The colours of my sleeve,
As for thy love I grieve.
maccauley_text_1917:
Let me show him these!
E'en the fisherwomen's sleeves
On Ojima's shores,
Though wet through and wet again,
Do not change their dyer's hues.

original_japanese:
きりぎりす
鳴くや霜夜の
さむしろに
衣かたしき
ひとりかも寝む
original_romaji:
Kirigirisu
Naku ya shimo yo no
Samushiro ni
Koromo katashiki
Hitori kamo nen
dickens_text_1866:
Now grasshopper's chirp the livelong night
I hear, now hoard-frost doth the ground
O'ercarpet, and in saddened plight,
My day-worn raiment yet unbound,
I strive in vain
On lonely couch reposo to gain.
noguchi_text_1907:
List, the crickets sing!
Upon the mat of the frost night,
I, my raiment not yet unbound.
Have to sleep alone.
porter_text_1909:
I'm sleeping all alone, and hear
The crickets round my head;
So cold and frosty is the night,
That I across the bed
My koromo have spread.
maccauley_text_1917:
On a chilling mat,
Drawing close my folded quilt,
I must sleep alone,
While all through the frosty night
Sounds a cricket's (forlorn chirp).

original_japanese:
わが袖は
潮干に見えぬ
沖の石の
人こそしらね
かはくまもなし
original_romaji:
Waga sode wa
Shiohi ni mienu
Oki no ishi no
Hito koso shirane
Kawaku ma mo nashi
dickens_text_1866:
My sleeve is as the rook unseen,
Ne'er bared at lowest ebb of tide,
And none do guess my grief, I ween,
Now how my tear-drenched sleeve's ne'er dried.
noguchi_text_1907:
My sleeves are like
The wide sea rocks unseen
Even at the lowest tide. Nobody would know
That their tears never dry.
porter_text_1909:
My sleeve is wet with floods of tears
As here I sit and cry;
’Tis wetter than a low-tide rock,—
No one, howe’er he try,
Can find a spot that 's dry!
maccauley_text_1917:
Like a rock at sea,
E'en at ebb-tide hid from view,
Is my tear-drenched sleeve:--
Never for a moment dry,
And unknown in human ken.

original_japanese:
世の中は
つねにもがもな
なぎさこぐ
あまの小舟の
綱手かなしも
original_romaji:
Yo no naka wa
Tsune ni mo ga mo na
Nagisa kogu
Ama no obune no
Tsuna de kanashi mo
dickens_text_1866:
O that throughout an endless life
I might in peace dwell, far from strive!
For ever watch the fishing yawl,
And view the nets abundant haul:
How fair to me,
How pleasant such a lot would be!
noguchi_text_1907:
Let my life be so!
Oh, to be carried away by the sight
Of a fisherman’s yawl at the shore,
And by his hauling of the net.
porter_text_1909:
I love to watch the fishing-boats
Returning to the bay,
The crew, all straining at the oars,
And coiling ropes away;
For busy folk are they.
maccauley_text_1917:
Would that this, our world,
Might be ever as it is!
What a lovely scene!
See that fisherwoman's boat,
Rope-drawn, rowed along the beach.

original_japanese:
みよし野の
山の秋風
さよふけて
ふるさとさむく
衣うつなり
original_romaji:
Miyoshino no
Yama no akikaze
Sayo fukete
Furusato samuku
Koromo utsu nari
dickens_text_1866:
Now autumn-gusts sweep
Down Miyoshino's steep,
And far into the night so drear
The sound of beating of the cloth,
Borne to me on the night-wind forth,
From my lonely village home, I hear.
noguchi_text_1907:
Down Miyoshino the Autumn wind blows,
The night is deep;
The beating sound of cloth
From my mountain home is cold.
porter_text_1909:
Around Mount Miyoshino's crest
The autumn winds blow drear;
The villagers are beating cloth,
Their merry din I hear,
This night so cold and clear.
maccauley_text_1917:
From Mount Yoshino
Blows a chill, autumnal wind,
In the deepening night.
Cold the ancient hamlet is;--
Sounds of beating cloth I hear.

original_japanese:
おほけなく
うき世の民に
おほふかな
わがたつそまに
墨染の袖
original_romaji:
Okenaku
Ukiyo no tami ni
Ou kana
Waga tatsu soma ni
Sumizome no sode
dickens_text_1866:
An ignorant man am I, unfit
O'er all the multitude of men
In dignity supreme to sit:
The simple priest's black robe again
I would, a humble dweller on
Wagatasoma, gladly don.
noguchi_text_1907:
Ah, to save the sad world,
Dare I attempt!
At this Wagatatsu Soma,
See my black-robed sleeves!
porter_text_1909:
Unfit to rule this wicked world
With all its pomp and pride,
I'd rather in my plain black robe
A humble priest abide,
Far up the mountain side.
maccauley_text_1917:
Though I am not fit,
I have dared to shield the folk
Of this woeful world
With my black-dyed (sacred) sleeve:--
I, who live on Mount Hiei.

original_japanese:
花さそふ
あらしの庭の
雪ならで
ふりゆくものは
わが身なりけり
original_romaji:
Hana sasou
Arashi no niwa no
Yuki nara de
Furi yuku mono wa
Waga mi nari keri
dickens_text_1866:
The court with Sakura's flowers is strewn
As thick as though the drifted snow
Did thereon lay: and I too soon
As withered low shall lie 'neath blow
Of man's inevitable foe.
noguchi_text_1907:
’Tis not the stormy snow
Luring the garden flower,
But what is falling fast
Is nothing but my own self.
porter_text_1909:
This snow is not from blossoms white
Wind-scattered, here and there,
That whiten all my garden paths
And leave the branches bare;
’Tis age that snows my hair!
maccauley_text_1917:
Not the snow of flowers,
That the hurrying wild-wind drags
Round the garden court,
Is it that here, withering, falls:--
That in truth is I, myself.

original_japanese:
こぬ人を
まつほの浦の
夕なぎに
やくやもしほの
身もこがれつつ
original_romaji:
Konu hito o
Matsuho no ura no
Yunagi ni
Yaku ya moshio no
Mi mo kogare tsutsu
dickens_text_1866:
On Matsu'ho's shore, our meeting place,
At dusky hour of night, I wait
My longed-for mistress to embrace;
Ah, why then linger'st thou so late!
My ardent passion, than the fire
That heats the salt-pans, rages higher.
noguchi_text_1907:
Ah, my heart pining
Like fire heats the salt water
In the evening calm of Matsuho shore!
Wouldn’t my love come?
porter_text_1909:
Upon the shore of Matsu-hō
For thee I pine and sigh;
Though calm and cool the evening air,
These salt-pans caked and dry
Are not more parched than I!
maccauley_text_1917:
Like the salt sea-weed,
Burning in the evening calm,
On Matsuo's shore,
All my being is aglow,
Waiting one who does not come.

original_japanese:
風そよぐ
ならの小川の
夕ぐれは
みそぎぞ夏の
しるしなりける
original_romaji:
Kaze soyogu
Nara no ogawa no
Yugure wa
Misogi zo natsu no
Shirushi nari keru
dickens_text_1866:
O'er Nara's streamlet softly blow
The winds in the now dim twilight,
the Misogi, thereby set, show
That summer hath not yet gone quite.
noguchi_text_1907:
The evening breeze blows
On the nara tree stream. To see
The Misogi feast might be the sign
Of Summer not yet gone.
porter_text_1909:
The twilight dim, the gentle breeze
By Nara's little stream,
The splash of worshippers who wash
Before the shrine, all seem
A perfect summer's dream.
maccauley_text_1917:
Lo! at Nara's brook
Evening comes, and rustling winds
Stir the oak-trees' leave;--
Not a sign of summer left
But the sacred bathing there.

original_japanese:
人も惜し
人も恨めし
あぢきなく
世を思ふゆゑに
もの思ふ身は
original_romaji:
Hito mo oshi
Hito mo urameshi
Ajiki naku
Yo o omou yue ni
Mono omou mi wa
dickens_text_1866:
Some men me love, some men me hate
Inspire: whene'er I think upon
This miserable world, my gate
My pitiable doth seem to me.
noguchi_text_1907:
I prize him
I resent him too
I deem this world miserable.
What wandering thought of mine?
porter_text_1909:
How I regret my fallen friends
How I despise my foes!
And, tired of life, I only seek
To reach my long day's close,
And gain at last repose.
maccauley_text_1917:
For some men I grieve;--
Some men are hateful to me;--
And this wretched world
To me, weighted down with care,
Is a place of misery.

original_japanese:
百敷や
古き軒端の
しのぶにも
なほあまりある
むかしなりけり
original_romaji:
Momoshiki ya
Furuki nokiba no
Shinobu ni mo
Nao amari aru
Mukashi nari keri
dickens_text_1866:
On th' hundred-chambered palace lo
A rent and tattered roof is seen,
Where rank Shinobu weeds do grow:--
How long, how hard out pain hath been!
noguchi_text_1907:
Alas, the palace!
See the Shinobu vine
On the olden eaves! Oh, what longing
For the by-gone days!
porter_text_1909:
My ancient Palace I regret,
Though rot attacks the eaves,
And o'er the roof the creeping vine
Spreads out and interweaves
Unpruned its straggling leaves.
maccauley_text_1917:
O Imperial House!
When I think of former days,
How I long for thee!
More than e'en the clinging vines
Hanging 'neath thine ancient eaves.
